source.title: Removing Information Content Does Not Certify Tamper Resistance in Open-Weight Models
source.authors: Domenic Rosati; Alessa Carbo; Ali Dadsetan; Hong Huang; Matthew Young; Subhabrata Majumdar; Frank Rudzicz; Hassan Sajjad

page_placements.theme: Recovery baselines: never-trained or retrained references also 'recover', and relearning speed reflects more than retained information

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including supplementary sections, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether information removal by itself predicts fine-tuning recovery, and its results and constructions argue that it does not certify slow recovery; recovery can vary with parameterization and training order.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites prior unlearning and recovery results, which are not recorded as this study's findings. Values used only to set a protocol or choose a threshold are not rows. Rows 1–12 report the study's own Deep Ignorance attacks; rows 13–26 report the zero-information factorized-head experiment; rows 27–30 cover theoretical and training-order results; rows 31–38 cover the BERT scrub and recovery experiment; rows 39–44 cover the supplementary Pythia-14M orbit experiment.
record.test_reason: The study's own experiments bear on three versions. A BERT-Tiny representation scrub brings target accuracy to the untrained level while keeping retain accuracy (A). Its fine-tuning recovery is slower than a never-adapted control in the released coordinates, but a function-preserving Q/K rescaling cuts seed-0 recovery from 280 to 25 steps (A, B). Fine-tuning attacks on the Deep Ignorance strong-filter checkpoint, a method claimed to be tamper-resistant, show its apparent resistance shrinks or disappears once the attacker rescales Q/K (F). The authors argue that information removal does not certify slow recovery. The factorized-head and toy results are authored constructions built to recover fast, not tests of an unlearning method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is right. Mutual information at release cannot by itself certify slow fine-tuning recovery. Exact information removal can coexist with fast recovery, and function-preserving reparameterization or training order can change recovery time, so a guarantee must also constrain attack dynamics. Two points should be added. The authors say Deep Ignorance's tamper-resistance results are artifacts of parameterization, though the body limits this to their runs and budget. They also frame the result as a limit on standalone certification, not on the usefulness of unlearning or filtering.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops information-theoretic and optimization-geometry analyses and tests data filtering, a BERT-Tiny scrub, and controlled zero-information constructions; it does not reproduce the named gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies with Q/K rescaling and factorized-head tangent scale; training order changes recovery in the scalar construction and the Pythia-160M experiments. The BERT comparison uses a fixed attack protocol and paired learning-rate grid.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing a target sample's training position changes recovery time while the scalar construction keeps weight–data MI fixed. Pythia-160M shows order-dependent recovery trends on AG News and E2E-NLG.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training order can change fine-tuning recovery time at fixed information content, without any unlearning intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed releases with exactly zero label–representation information recover fast. A toy release recovers in one gradient step (Prop. 5.3), and a factorized head on frozen Pythia-160M recovers in 1–306 SGD steps for s ≥ 0.02. Smaller s are censored only because the fixed rate gives an effective rate of eta*s^2. Two zero-MI minimizers of the same removal objective differ: one recovers in one step, the other is stationary.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zero information at release does not lower-bound fine-tuning recovery time; recovery speed is set by parameterization and the chosen minimizer, not information content.

fits_no_version.finding: Function-preserving Q/K rescaling of pretrained Pythia-14M changes the time to relearn 128 random item–token associations: 865 to 1,825 steps across six scales, single seed, no unlearning applied.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning speed varies along function-preserving parameter orbits, independent of any unlearning.

record.code_released: not stated; the checklist says code and data will be released upon publication, but gives no URL.
record.problems: The paper's exact-zero-information recovery constructions are controlled mathematical or restricted-head examples, not tests of named LLM unlearning methods. The BERT paired Q/K recovery comparison is single-seed and does not establish complete MI removal. The factorized-head positive-scale failures are budget-censored and depend on the fixed learning rate. The Deep Ignorance attacks are three-seed, one-epoch comparisons. Pythia-160M figure values and Pythia-14M scale-specific hitting times are not stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4's Fashion-MNIST experiment reports a 21-point orbit sweep graphically without text-stated scale-specific recovery times; it is omitted because the 60-row cap is reached only after prioritizing text-stated and table-reported results. The figure's setup and qualitative purpose are described in Supp. A.

untested.parts: Named LLM unlearning methods (RMU, gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter) and WMDP-style unlearned LLMs. Only a BERT-Tiny MSE scrub on AG News is tested, and general ability is measured only as AG News retain-class accuracy. No attack other than fine-tuning on target data is run.
Small, unrelated or loosely related relearning sets, and recovery from a subset of the forgotten facts. Recovery here fine-tunes on the full target-class training data.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deleting. The only internal analysis is a logistic-probe V-information estimate after the scrub (see missing).
Prompting, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context attacks are not tested.

Only Deep Ignorance strong-filter pretraining filtering is examined, with one 293-update SGD epoch on WMDP-bio items. UF was not rescaled upward, so there is no same-scale comparison of the best attack on each checkpoint. No pre-attack accuracies are reported, and no other robust methods (e.g. TAR, weight-space regularization) are tested.

missing.what: Information-removal result for the BERT scrub: logistic-probe V-information falls from 0.433/0.449/0.457 to 0.178/0.150/0.115 nats (embedding/L1/L2), vs 0.140/0.139/0.140 for a matched random encoder. These are decoder-class estimates, not Shannon MI. This bears on A's removal criterion beyond accuracy, and no row records it.

record.verdict_notes: Read the full text (about 1,500 lines including Supp A, B.1–B.4 and Tables 1–3). The text contains no instructions to the reader. Changes from the previous verdict: (1) Every row carrying V-names now has its own row_fixes item with declared letters: R1–R12 to F; R13–R26 and R28 to none; R31, R37 and R38 to A; R32–R36 to A and B. The earlier single R13 item covering R14–R26 is expanded into one item per row. R38 had no item and gets A, observed. (2) R34 changed from observed to partial to match R33, which is the same measure. (3) R11 changed from observed to partial, because SF's lag is one 25-update logging interval. (4) R32 and R36 are now linked to A as well as B, since A's verdict uses the controls; R32 was added to A's label. (5) R37's problem text is corrected: the paper never says 'near chance'; the untrained arms sit at about 50%. (6) Label reasons are tightened: F notes that UF was never run at alpha=8; B notes that the control was not rescaled. (7) The empty fits_no_version entry is removed and two entries are added (the zero-information constructions, and the Pythia-14M orbit). (8) The empty authors_conclusion is filled in. (9) One missing entry is added for the BERT V-information probe result. Rows R27, R29, R30 and R39–R44 already carry 'none' and are left as they are. Multi-version rows carry a single state: R35 is partial because it is one seed with an unrescaled control; read separately, A's slowdown is gone there and B's recovery beats fresh learning.

versions.untested_parts: Only the BERT-Tiny MSE scrub is tested as a capability-removal intervention; the paper does not evaluate gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or other named unlearning methods. Its scrub is near chance on target accuracy and preserves retain accuracy, but recovery is measured after fine-tuning.

Tests include recovery fine-tuning after a BERT scrub and after exact zero-information constructions, and fine-tuning attacks after filtering. The paper does not test recovery using a few unrelated examples or compare different sizes or relatedness levels of relearning sets.
No activation-direction ablation is performed, and the study does not test a particular unlearning method's blocking of access versus deletion.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
The study does not propose or evaluate a newer method that resists the listed attacks.

source_check.notes: Deep Ignorance: 3 seeds, one epoch, only 100 held-out items, and UF was not run at alpha=8. The intro calls O'Brien et al.'s results 'simply artifacts', but the body limits this to these runs, and a 6-point held-out gap remains. The BERT-Tiny rescale is a single seed, and its control was neither rescaled nor utility-matched. No code is released yet.

statements.correction: Scrub: target accuracy 91.7% -> 53.4 ± 3.6%, retain 96.3 ± 1.2%. Recovery takes 252 ± 67 updates. That is slower than the never-adapted control (75 ± 5; not utility-matched, retain 34.1 ± 15.3%) and faster than random init (>1,000). Only the single-seed alpha=32 rescale (25 vs 280 steps) beats the control, which was not rescaled. A verdict: limits_scope.
statements.problem: BERT-Tiny numbers are right. But the group heading ('unlearned models relearn the target quickly' against a never-trained reference) and the label 'challenges' do not fit this study. Its 3-seed scrub relearns more slowly than the never-adapted control, and its A verdict is limits_scope.

statements.correction: Drop the 2610.09004 citation (R34, R35), or state it separately as an attack-side parameterization factor: exact Q/K rescaling of one scrubbed BERT-Tiny checkpoint changes seed-0 recovery from 280 to 25 steps. No layer, retain-set or stopping-rule factor is tested.
statements.problem: The statement gives no fact about this study. Its factor is unlearning configuration (layer, depth, retain set, stopping/selection). The cited R34 and R35 are attack-side Q/K rescaling of one fixed scrubbed checkpoint, which is none of these.
Makes no specific claim about this study and cites no rows from it. Its verdict counts include this study's A limits_scope, which stands. Nothing conflicts with the text.

statements.correction: Fine-tuning restores the criterion (target accuracy >=75%, CE <=0.5) in 252 ± 67 updates. That is slower than the never-adapted control (75 ± 5; retain 34.1 vs 96.3%) and faster than random init (>1,000). Seed 0: 280 steps unscaled, 25 at alpha=32; the control was not rescaled. B verdict: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The numbers and the 'not utility-matched' caveat are right, and the 3-seed scrub indeed shows no recovery advantage over the never-adapted control. But it is listed under 'challenges', while the study's B verdict is limits_scope. It also omits the seed-0 rescaled run, which recovers in 25 steps and beats the control.

All this study's numbers match B.1 and Sec 4 (58.5 ± 5.0, 68.9 ± 1.8, 69.3 ± 4.4, median 125, gap 14.7 -> 6.0, 54.0 vs 60.0, UF not run at alpha=8). Minor: 'without instruction tuning' is not stated in this text.

statements.correction: Rescaled SF (alpha=8): 69.3 ± 4.4% training accuracy after 293 updates; median 125 updates to the first logged training accuracy >=60%.
statements.problem: 'SF reaches 69.3 ± 4.4% in 125 updates' merges two measures. 69.3% is final training accuracy after 293 updates; 125 is the median first logged update with training accuracy >=60%. Everything else is right.
Matches B.1 (training 58.5 vs 69.3; held-out 45.3 vs 54.0; one SGD epoch).
This study's numbers match (58.5, 69.3, 68.9 training; 54.0 vs 60.0 held-out). The held-out gap is correctly reported as remaining.
All numbers, the verdict summary and the open point (UF not run at alpha=8) match the text. 'No code' fits: code is to be released on publication.
Toy release recovers in one step (Prop 5.3). '1-306' is the range of median hitting steps for s >= 0.02 (per-seed max at s=0.02 is 311). Smaller s values are censored at 500.
